introduction.p: Euler's method advances with one slope at the start of a step. Runge–Kutta methods sample additional slopes to approximate the change more accurately. This optional section compares explicit Euler, improved Euler (Heun), midpoint, and classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta methods. It assumes an initial value problem with a smooth solution on the interval being computed.

subsection.title: Two slopes and four slopes
subsection.p: For y'=F(t,y), use a step from (t_n,y_n) to t_n+h. Explicit Euler is y_{n+1}=y_n+hF(t_n,y_n). Heun's method predicts with Euler and averages the initial and predicted final slopes:
The explicit midpoint method uses the initial slope to predict the midpoint, then uses its slope for the whole step:
Both are second-order methods, but they need not give the same value on a nonlinear equation. Here the k_i are slopes; the factor h is applied when forming changes.

The two midpoint slopes are evaluated at different predicted values of y. Replacing one by the other changes the method. For a system, apply the same formulas to vector values, evaluating all components of each stage together.

subsection.title: Local error and accumulated error
subsection.p: The one-step local error is the difference between an exact solution value at the end of a step and one numerical step started from the exact value at its beginning. A method has order p when this error is O(h^{p+1}) and its accumulated, or global, error over a fixed finite interval is O(h^p). Here O(h^r) means a magnitude bounded by a constant times h^r for all sufficiently small positive h, with the constant independent of the step size. Some texts divide the local error by h; here we do not.

For the following orders, assume F and its partial derivatives through order four are continuous and bounded in a neighborhood containing the exact and numerical trajectories, and one constant L\ge0 satisfies |F(t,u)-F(t,v)|\le L|u-v| there. This is the Lipschitz condition in the dependent variable. A partial derivative in t or y means varying that input while holding the other fixed. The initial value is exact, the interval length is fixed, and the stated orders describe exact arithmetic as h\to0.

To see the second-order match, write F_t,F_y for the two derivatives at the starting point. Along an exact solution, y''=F_t+F_yF. Expanding the final slope in Heun's method gives k_2=F+h(F_t+F_yF)+O(h^2); its averaged update is y+hF+\tfrac12h^2(F_t+F_yF)+O(h^3), matching the exact Taylor expansion through degree two. The midpoint calculation gives the same degree-two match.

For RK4, Taylor expansion of all four stages matches the exact solution through degree four. One compact way to state this calculation is to define DG=G_t+FG_y for any smooth function G(t,y). The exact change and the RK4 change both have the expansion
with all terms evaluated at the start. Here D^2F=D(DF) and D^3F=D(D^2F). The weights alone are not a quadrature proof: the predicted stage values must also produce this Taylor match.

The loss of one power in global error comes from accumulating about 1/h steps. More precisely, smoothness gives a one-step perturbation bound 1+Ch for some fixed C\ge0. If the local error is at most Kh^{p+1}, then the global errors satisfy e_{n+1}\le(1+Ch)e_n+Kh^{p+1}. Iterating this inequality over nh\le T gives e_n\le KTh^p e^{CT} when e_0=0. This explains why local accuracy needs both smoothness and control of error propagation.

example.title: A reproducible accuracy comparison
example.p: For y'=y, y(0)=1, the exact endpoint is y(1)=e. With h=1/n, the one-step multipliers are 1+h for Euler, 1+h+h^2/2 for Heun and midpoint, and 1+h+h^2/2+h^3/6+h^4/24 for RK4. Raise each multiplier to the n-th power to reproduce these endpoint absolute errors:

Halving the step eventually divides the error by roughly 2, 4, and 16, respectively. At equal slope-evaluation cost, compare Euler with 4n steps, Heun with 2n steps, and RK4 with n steps; equal step counts alone do not give equal work.

warning.title: Higher order does not remove stability restrictions
warning.p: For y'=\lambda y, RK4 advances with multiplier P(z)=1+z+z^2/2+z^3/6+z^4/24, where z=h\lambda. On y'=-4y, choosing h=1 gives P(-4)=5, so the numerical values grow although the exact solution decays. A higher-order explicit method still needs a suitable step. Nonsmooth laws, long time intervals, rapidly decaying components, and roundoff require separate attention.

statement.p: Approximate y(1) for y'=t+y, y(0)=1, using Euler with 16 steps, Heun with 8, and RK4 with 4. Each uses 16 slope evaluations. Compare with y(t)=2e^t-t-1. Repeat with twice as many evaluations. Also verify the RK4 multiplier on the test equation.

hint.p: Use the correct time in every stage. Expected error ratios approach 2,4,16 as the step shrinks. Successive substitutions in the four stages give the degree-four polynomial multiplier.
